# Results — Study 490 (Arms Index / TRIN)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a high TRIN
marks a panic/washout and precedes a short-term bounce** — encoded as a mechanical rule. TRIN is
built from a **breadth proxy** (each basket ETF is one "issue", |return| stands in for issue
volume; see the caveat below); a long fires when TRIN exceeds its 90th percentile (the panic
tail), read on the close of t and entered at the **next close** (one documented lag), and we
measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return on SPY. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for the basket **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-04 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| TRIN | breadth-proxy Arms index, median **0.86**, q90 **4.25** (panic threshold) |
| Entries | **461** high-TRIN panic spikes (q = 0.90), traded on SPY |
| Timing / costs | TRIN read on close of t; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per entry |

> **Breadth caveat (this caps the test).** True TRIN uses *exchange-wide* advancing/declining
> issue counts and their volumes. That feed is unavailable offline, so we build a coarse
> **5-issue breadth proxy** from the cached ETF basket: an ETF advances if its daily return > 0,
> and |return| substitutes for issue volume, with a small volume floor + Laplace count prior so
> tiny-move days don't blow the ratio up. The top-TRIN days the proxy flags are the real
> washouts (16/12 Mar 2020, Dec 2008), so the proxy is directionally sane — but it is *not* the
> NYSE TRIN, and a 5-issue breadth measure is much noisier than 3000 issues. The Signal question
> is unchanged: does the breadth signal beat **random-day** entries on SPY?

## The signal — high-TRIN panic entry vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch panic-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = panic − random.

| horizon | n | panic | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (panic−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 461 | +49.2 bps | 61% | +2.94 | +19.8 bps | **+29.4 bps** | +47.2 bps | +1.53 | 0.126 |
| 10-day | 460 | +77.4 bps | 63% | +3.42 | +49.8 bps | **+27.6 bps** | +75.4 bps | +1.12 | 0.263 |
| 20-day | 460 | +138.2 bps | 67% | +3.71 | +104.9 bps | **+33.3 bps** | +136.2 bps | +1.04 | 0.299 |
| 60-day | 454 | +326.8 bps | 72% | +3.79 | +278.6 bps | **+48.2 bps** | +324.8 bps | +0.90 | 0.370 |

Read it carefully. Unlike most technical rules on this desk, the panic entry is **positive
against the drift-matched random baseline at every horizon** (Δ = +29/+28/+33/+48 bps) — TRIN is
not pure beta. But the panic-minus-random difference **never clears the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar** (max
Welch *t* = +1.53 at 5 days, *p* = 0.126). So the bounce-after-panic effect is **real in sign and
direction but statistically weak** once the free drift is removed — a hint, not a confirmed edge.

## Threshold sweep (H = 10) — the panic tail is monotone, not cherry-picked

| panic cutoff | n | panic | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (panic−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| q = 0.80 | 836 | +70.5 bps | +4.27 | +44.0 bps | **+26.5 bps** |
| q = 0.90 | 461 | +77.4 bps | +3.42 | +49.8 bps | **+27.6 bps** |
| q = 0.95 | 245 | +83.9 bps | +2.50 | +61.2 bps | **+22.7 bps** |

The panic-bounce premium (panic − random ≈ +23 to +28 bps over 10 days) is **stable across the
threshold** — it isn't an artifact of one cherry-picked cutoff. Higher cutoffs raise the raw
panic return but thin the sample, so the delta is roughly flat.

## Timing placebo — scramble *when* the panic days fall, and the result collapses

The decisive "does the *timing* matter?" test: permute the TRIN series in time (same marginal,
same number of panic days at the same threshold) so high-TRIN days fall on random dates. If the
alignment of high-TRIN days with subsequent bounces is real, the scramble should demolish it.

| horizon | observed panic return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | +49.2 bps | **0.001** | 1000 |
| 10-day | +77.4 bps | **0.007** | 1000 |
| 20-day | +138.2 bps | **0.009** | 1000 |
| 60-day | +326.8 bps | **0.041** | 1000 |

Here is the twist that keeps this off the None pile: the real high-TRIN timing **beats >95% of
scrambled-timing nulls at every horizon** (*p* = 0.001 → 0.041). The *placement* of the panic
days carries genuine information — high-TRIN days really do cluster ahead of rebounds. The
tension with the weak Welch test above is honest and instructive: the placebo null (same panic
marginal, shuffled in time) is *weaker* than the drift-matched random baseline, so the same
effect that clears the placebo fails to clear the harder vs-random bar. The signal is real but
small — and most of it is the volatility-rebound that any "buy after a crash day" rule captures.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a planted bounce

On a deterministic basket with a *planted* post-panic bounce (knob `edge`; synchronised down-days
spike TRIN, then name A rebounds after entry), the same panic rule behaves as it must — so the
real-tape result is a genuine measurement, not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | panic | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no bounce) | 353 | +30.3 bps | 54% | +1.25 |
| **0.60** (real planted bounce) | 358 | +66.3 bps | 59% | **+2.72** |

At edge = 0 the control averages to a coin across seeds (mean *t* ≈ 0; this single seed lands at
+1.25, within sampling noise); a planted bounce lights up at *t* = +2.72 with a 59% win-rate. The
detector is live.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The high-TRIN panic entry **beats** a drift-matched random baseline at every
  horizon (Δ = +29/+28/+33/+48 bps at 5/10/20/60 days) and the timing placebo is significant
  (*p* = 0.001–0.041), so there is a **real** bounce-after-panic effect — TRIN is *not* just beta.
  But the panic-minus-random Welch *t* **never clears 2** (max +1.53, *p* = 0.13): the edge is
  directionally real yet statistically weak once the free drift is stripped.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** A ~25–30 bps per-trade premium over random survives a 1 bp round-trip
  cost almost untouched, but it rests on ~460 clustered crash-period entries, never reaches *t* =
  2, and is dominated by the generic volatility-rebound (any "buy the crash day" rule grabs most
  of it). It is a hint a careful tape-reader might lean on, not a stand-alone, scalable edge.
- **"Does TRIN forecast short-term turns?" — MIXED.** The placebo says yes — the *timing* of
  high-TRIN days carries genuine information ahead of rebounds (p ≤ 0.04 at every horizon). The
  vs-random Welch test says *not strongly* — the effect doesn't clear the desk's significance bar.
  Real structure, weak forecast: a panic gauge that leans the right way without paying its way to
  a confident "Confirmed".
